title: Micrometeorite puncture detection and repair
bottleneck: Habitat pressure hulls will be struck by micrometeorites traveling kilometers per second; small punctures may leak slowly enough to be survivable, but locating a millimeter-scale hole in a large habitat — in vacuum, possibly under regolith shielding — is genuinely hard. Self-healing materials exist only as lab curiosities, and EVA repair of a hull buried under shielding is operationally nightmarish. A slow leak that cannot be found is a slow death sentence for the air supply.
why_it_blocks: Loss of pressure is the fastest-killing habitat failure mode; without reliable find-and-fix, every habitat must carry massive air reserves or accept evacuation-level risk from a single grain of dust.
current_state: The ISS uses Whipple shields and leak isolation by module; patch kits exist for accessible areas. Autonomous leak localization and self-repairing hulls remain research topics.
